49. Christ. CATECHESIS It starts from Hebr 1,1 ss: «God spoke many times and in many ways in the past to our Fathers through the Prophets; In these last times he has spoken to us through the Son..."1. Christ, superior to all others anointed as the only and eternal Son of God the Father

1. What we told you yesterday sufficiently explains, for our part, that we hope in Jesus Christ. But we must not believe in Jesus Christ in a simple and vulgar way, nor must we accept him as any one of the many who, in an abusive way, have been called "Christs." They were "Christs" as a type and image, but this is the true Christ, who was not chosen from among men and promoted to the priesthood, but received priestly dignity from the eternal Father. That is why faith warns us not to think that it is any of the ordinary (anointed) "Christs": to the confession of faith we add that we believe "in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only son of God." Son of God the Father by nature

2. When you hear about the Son, do not think of adoption, but of a Son by nature, an Only Begotten Son who has no other brother. That is why he is called Only Begotten, because he has no brother in the dignity of the deity and in the paternal generation. But we do not call him the Son of God out of our own impulse, but because the Father himself gave him the name Son, and the name that parents give to their children is true. Peter, on behalf of the apostles, recognizes Jesus as the Son of God

3. Our Lord Jesus Christ put on human nature at that time, but this was unknown to many. When he, knowing that it was unknown, wanted to teach it, gathering the disciples he asked them: "Who do men say the Son of Man is?" (Mt 16,13). He did not seek ephemeral glory, but he wanted to tell them the truth so that it would not happen that, while they were living with the only begotten Son of God, and God himself, they would despise him as a simple man. When they say: «... some, that Elijah; others, that Jeremiah" (16,14), it is as if he answered them: those who do not know have an excuse but you, who are apostles and heal lepers in my name, cast out demons and bring the dead back to life, you must know who it is for whom you perform these wonders. When everyone was reluctant (since this reality exceeded human strength), Peter, prince of the apostles and supreme preacher of the Church, did not use his own words or human reasoning, but, flooded with light in his mind illuminated by the Father, he said to him: "You are the Christ" (Mt 16:16), adding: "The Son of the living God" (ibid.). And immediately a declaration of blessedness is added (superior to what man can grasp), made up of the affirmation that it was a revelation from the Father. For the Savior says: “Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah, because it was not flesh and blood that revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven (16:17). Thus, whoever recognizes our Lord Jesus Christ as the Son of God, is made a participant in the beatitude; but whoever denies the Son of God becomes unhappy and miserable3. Son in everything similar to the Father

4. When he is called Son, do not think that it is an exaggeration, but that he is truly a son, by nature, without a beginning. He has not passed from servitude to adoption, but is a Son begotten from all eternity, through an inscrutable and unfathomable process of generation. In a similar way, when you hear about "firstborn" (cf. Hebr 1:6), do not understand it in a human way, because men also have other brothers, and somewhere it is said: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Ex 4:22). But just as Reuben was stripped of his honor as Jacob's firstborn for having entered his parents' bed, Israel also crucified the Son by throwing him out of the vineyard of God the Father (Mt 21:39 sqq.)4. And to others the Scripture says: "You are children of Yahweh your God" (Dt 14:1). And, in another place: «I had said: "You are gods, all of you, children of the Most High!"» (Ps 82,6)6. It says: "I said," and not: "I have begotten." For they received by the voice and word of God the adoption that they did not have. But he (the Messiah) did not go from being one thing to becoming another, but from the beginning he was born as the Son of the Father, existing before any beginning and before the centuries. He is the Son of the Father in everything similar to his progenitor; eternal from the eternal Father, begotten as life from life, light from light, truth from truth, wisdom from wisdom, King from King, God from God, power from power. Eternal generation of the Son

5. When you hear the Gospel that says: "Book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham" (Mt 1:1), understand this in relation to the flesh. For he is truly the son of David forever, but he is the Son of God before all ages and without a beginning7. And he truly assumed what he did not have8, but what he has he has from eternity as begotten of the Father. He has two fathers: one, David, according to the flesh; the other, according to divinity, God the Father. What he has from David is subject to time, it can be verified and it is a lineage that can be detailed, but what comes from divinity is not subject to time or space, nor does it have an ancestry that can be accounted for: "Who cares about his ancestry?"9. God is spirit, and what is spirit is generated spiritually, in an incorporeal way without any lineage being traceable. The Son himself says of the Father: «He said to me: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you..."» (Ps 2:7). That "today" does not express something recent, but eternal. It is a "today" without time, before all centuries: "... From the womb before the dawn I have begotten you" (Ps 110,3, classical Greek version). Believe in the Son of God

6. Believe, therefore, in Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, the only begotten Son, according to the Gospel, which says: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (Jn 3:16). And, in turn: "He who believes in him (the Son) is not judged" (3:18), but has "passed from death to life" (I Jn 3:14). But "he who refuses to believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (Jn 3:36), "because he has not believed in the Name of the only Son of God" (Jn 3:18). John bore witness to him saying: "We have contemplated his glory, glory that he receives from the Father as the only Son, full of grace and truth" (Jn 1:14). In fear of him the demons said: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of God Most High" (Mk 5:7; cf. Lk 4:34). The Father begets the Son in the highest perfection 10

7. Therefore, the Son of God is by nature and not by adoption, begotten by the Father. But he who loves him who begot him also loves him who he has begotten. But he who despises the one begotten by him transmits his affront to his progenitor. And when you hear about God begetting, do not think about bodily generation, nor think about reproduction that involves corruption, lest you fall into impiety. "God is spirit" (Jn 4:24) and his generation is spiritual; for bodies, for their part, beget bodies and in bodily generation there must be a passage of time. However, in the generation of the Son from the Father there is no temporal interval. Furthermore, when something is generated, it is generated as an imperfect reality; However, the Son of God has been begotten as perfect: existing today, existing from the beginning, born without a beginning. In this way we are born, passing after childhood ignorance to the use of reason: imperfect is your birth, O man, although growth is produced through successive additions. But in the case at hand, do not think anything like that or any weakness of the parent come to mind, (as if you were saying): he begat someone imperfect who, as time passed, achieved perfection. You accuse the parent of weakness by saying that what was later granted by the passage of time had not been given, in your opinion, from the beginning.

8. Do not believe, therefore, that it is a human generation or similar to how Abraham begat Isaac. For Abraham did not father Isaac because he wanted to, but because someone other than him granted it to him. When it is God and Father who generates, there is no ignorance nor deliberation. And to say that he did not know what he engendered is extremely impious. To say also that he was weighing the circumstances and then began to be a father is also impiety of the same category: for it is not that God first existed without children and then, at a certain moment, became a father, but that he has always had the Son. He begot him, not as men beget men, but as he alone knew him, who begat him before all ages as true God.

9. Therefore being the true God the Father, he begot a Son, the true God, like unto himself. And not as teachers have disciples, that is, not as Paul says to some: "It was I who, through the Gospel, begot you in Christ Jesus" (I Cor 4:15). For he who was not a son by nature has become one as a disciple. But in the case in question it is a son by nature, a true son. Nor as you, who are to be enlightened, are now made children of God; for you also have been made children, but in adoption by grace, according to what is written: “To all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name. They were not born of blood, nor of the desire of the flesh, nor of the desire of man, but they were born of God" (Jn I, 12-13)11. And we are certainly born of water and the Spirit (cf. Jn 3:5), but this is not how Christ was born of the Father. Remember that at the moment of baptism the voice said: "This is my son" (Mt 3:17; cf. 17:5), and not: "This has now become my Son." By saying "This is my Son," he declared that he was already a Son before the baptism was performed.

10. The Father did not beget the Son as the mind generates the word in men. For in us the mind is something subsistent, but the word that is pronounced is lost in the air. We have known, however, that Christ was born not simply as a word that is pronounced, but as a subsistent and living Word, not uttered and spread with the lips, but engendered from the eternal Father in an ineffable way and with a solid subsistence12. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and the Word was God" (Jn 1:1), seated on the right (cf. Ps 110:1). Word that understands the will of the Father, Word that builds everything according to his good pleasure, Word that descends and ascends (cf. Eph 4:10)13. But a word, when it is uttered, does not go down and up as it is pronounced, but is expressed by saying: "I speak what I have seen with my Father" (Jn 8:38). It is a Word full of authority and that exercises dominion over all things, since the Father has handed everything over to the Son (cf. Jn 13:3 and Mt 11:27)14.

11. The Father begot him, but not as anyone understood, but as he alone knows15. Well, we will not hesitate to explain how it came about. We can only talk about what that generation has not been like. It is true that the Son proceeds from the Father, although also all nature begotten or created. "Ask the earth and it will tell you" (Job 12:8 Hebrew). Even if you question everything on earth, they will not be able to tell you. And the globe cannot explain who its modeler or its creator is. And not only is the earth unaware of it, but also the sun is unaware of it. For the sun was created on the fourth day without knowing what had been created on the previous three days. But anyone who did not know what was done in the three days before him obviously cannot say who the author was. Nor will heaven say it, since it was placed by Christ, by the will of the Father, as if it were a cloud of smoke. Neither will the heavens of heaven nor the waters that are above the heavens tell it. Why, then, do you lament, O man, that you do not know what the heavens themselves do not know? And it is not only the heavens that ignore this generation, but even the angelic creatures do not know it. If someone - assuming it were possible - ascended to the first heaven and, upon observing the place of the angels who dwell there16, approaching, asked how God begot his Son, perhaps he would answer: Higher up there are those greater and higher than us. Ask them. Climb up to the second and third heavens: reach, if you can, up to the thrones and dominions, and also the principalities and powers. If someone got there - it is impossible - they would give up describing them, since they would not even have explored them.

12. I have always been amazed at the curiosity of some who, by giving reckless opinions on religious issues, fall into impiety. They think that the thrones and dominions, created by Christ, and also the principalities and powers17 are undiscovered, and thus they try to discover the Creator with greater curiosity18. Tell me first of all, you who are very daring, what difference there is between throne and domination. Seek then the things that concern Christ. Tell me what is a “principality” and a “power” or what is a “power” and an angel. He then curiously investigates the Creator, since "everything was made through him" (cf. Jn 1:3). But you don't want to interrogate the thrones and dominions or maybe it's more that you can't. And, who is there who knows the depths of God but the Holy Spirit (cf. 1 Cor 2:10-11), who is the one who spoke in the Scriptures? But not even the Holy Spirit Himself spoke in the Scriptures of (I mode of) the generation of the Son by the Father. Why do you diligently investigate what not even the Holy Spirit himself described in the Scriptures? And if you ignore what has been written, will you be able to investigate the things that have not been written? There are many questions that Scripture deals with: if we cannot cover what is written, why tire our spirits with what is not written? It is enough for us to know that God begot an only Son.

13. Do not be ashamed to confess your ignorance when in it you have something in common with the angels19. Only he who begot knows him who begotten, and he who was begotten by him knows his progenitor. And he who has begotten knows what he has begotten. And the Holy Spirit of God testifies in Scripture that the begotten is God without there having been a beginning. «Indeed, what man knows the innermost part of the man that is in him? In the same way, no one knows the inner things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor 2:11). "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself" (Jn 5:26). And, furthermore, "so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father" (5:23). And: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes" (5:21). And neither the one who begets is diminished in anything nor the one begotten lacks anything (I know that I have already spoken of these things)20. But it is for our safety that these things have been frequently repeated. Neither he who begot has a father nor does he who begotten have a brother. Neither the begetter became a son in this way nor the begotten became a father. From one Father an only Son has been begotten. It is not about two unborn children or two only begotten children. But there is only one unbegotten Father (unbegotten is he who has no Father) and there is only one Son, eternally begotten by the Father: not born in time, but begotten before the ages: and who also has not experienced growth, but has been begotten as he currently is.

14. We believe, therefore, in the only begotten Son of God, born of the Father as true God21. For a true God does not beget a false god, as has already been said. Nor did he generate after having deliberated with himself, but he did so from eternity in a much faster way, logically, than our words and our thoughts. For we, when we speak in time, use time, but, when we speak of divine power, the act of generating is outside of time. And, as has been said very often, it is not that he brought the Son from non-existence to being, nor did he receive him who was not in adoption; but the Father, who existed from eternity, eternally and unspeakably begot his only Son, who had no other brother. Nor are there two principles, but the head of the Son is the Father22, which is the only principle. Thus, the Father begot the Son as true God, called "Immanuel", which, understanding it correctly, is translated as "God with us" (cf. Mt 1:23)23

15. Do you want to realize that it is God who was born from the Father and then became man? Listen to the prophet: “This is our God, no other is comparable to him. He discovered the whole way of knowledge, and taught it to his servant Jacob, and to Israel his beloved. Then she appeared on earth, and lived among men" (Bar 3:36-38). Do you think that God, after the Law of Moses, did not become man? It also welcomes another testimony of the divinity of Christ just read: "Your throne, O God, forever and ever" (Ps 45:7). And so that in connection with these passages it would not be thought that with his coming in the flesh he later reached, as if by development, the summit of divinity, he says openly: "For this reason God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of joy more than your companions." Don't you see that the Messiah God has been anointed by God the Father?

16. Do you also want to be offered a third testimony of the divinity of Christ? Hear Isaiah say: "The products of Egypt, the trade of Kush... will come to you and will be yours"; and shortly after: «They will prostrate themselves before you and beg you: "In you alone there is God, there is no other, there are no more gods." Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, savior” (Is 45,1415)24. You see God the Son who has God the Father in himself. He only needs to say what he said in the Gospels: "I am in the Father and the Father is in me" (Jn 14:11). He does not say "I am the Father," but rather "I am in the Father and the Father is in me." And, in turn, he did not say: "I and the Father are one", but "I and the Father are one" (Jn 10:30), so that we neither separate them one from the other, nor make a mixture of Father and Son. "One", because the dignity of divinity is one, since it is God who begot God. "One" by the prerogative of the Kingdom, since it is not that the Father reigns over some things and the Son reigns over others, as if the latter, like Absalom25, stood against the Father. In reality, the Son reigns over the same things that the Father reigns over. They are "one" also because there is no dissonance or separation, since one is not the desires of the Father and the other is those of the Son. "One" because there are not some works of Christ and others those of the Father. The ordering of all things is unitary, since the Father has acted through the Son: «For he spoke and so it was; He commanded and they were created” (Ps 148,5 LXX), says the psalmist. But he who says, says to him who hears; and whoever commands, commands whoever is present.

17. The Son is, therefore, true God, having the Father in himself, but not transformed into the Father: for neither did the Father become man, but the Son—let us say it truly and freely. The Father did not suffer for us, but the Father sent him who suffered for us. Nor should we ever say: "There was a time in which the Son did not exist."26 Let us also not admit a filio-paternity, but let us advance along the royal path without deviating to the left or to the right. Nor, believing we honor the Son, let us call him Father nor, thinking of paying honor to the Father, let us believe that the Son is one of the created things. Rather the one Father is worshiped through the only Son, without worship being "distributed." Preach an only Son, seated at the right hand of the Father before the centuries, who has not received in time this sitting with the Father after suffering and as a result of evolution, but who has possessed it from eternity.

18. "He who sees the Son, sees the Father"27. For in everything the Son is like unto him who begat him: life from life, light from light, power from power, God from God. The characteristics of the divinity in the Son are in no way different, and whoever has been considered worthy of seeing the divinity of the Son has been thereby led to enjoy the Father. This way of speaking is not mine, but that of the only begotten Son: «Have I been with you so long and you do not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father” (Jn 14:9)29. And, to put it more compendiously, we must avoid both separating and confusing: never say that the Son is alien to the Father nor accept those who say that the Father is sometimes Father and sometimes Son: these are strange and impious statements, not testimonies of the Church, since the Father remained such even if he had begotten the Son without undergoing transformation himself. He begot Wisdom (cf. I Cor 1:24), but he was not deprived of her; It engendered strength without losing its energy. By begetting God, he was not stripped of his divinity nor did he lose anything, being diminished or transformed, nor does the begotten lack anything: perfect is the one who begot and perfect is the begotten. God is the one who begot and God is the one who has been begotten, who is God of all things and calls his God Father, without fear of saying: "I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (Jn 20:17).

19. But so that you do not believe that this is an equal paternity for both the Son and the other creatures, in the sentences that follow he made a distinction. For he did not say: "I ascend to our Father," so that a community of creatures with the Only Begotten could be deduced; but says: "my Father and your Father." In a way, mine, by nature; and in another way, yours, by adoption. And, in turn: "To my God and your God." In a way, my Father by natural bond and as only begotten Son; otherwise, yours as creatures. Therefore, the Son of God is true God, begotten in an ineffable way before all ages. I often repeat all this to you so that it is well recorded in your mind. Certainly believe that God has a Son, but do not be too curious about how, because if you inquire you will not find an answer. Do not exalt yourself, lest you fall. Simply surrender to the meditation of what is entrusted to you. Tell me who the one who begot really is and you will then realize what he begot. If with thought you cannot encompass the nature of the one who begets, do not scrutinize with impatience who the begotten is.

20. For piety it is enough for you to know that we said that God has an only Son: a Son begotten by nature, who did not begin to exist when He was born in Bethlehem, but before all centuries. Listen, in fact, to the prophet Micah, who says: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, although you are the least among the families of Judah, from you will come forth one who will rule in Israel, and whose origins are of old, from the days of old" (Micah 5:1). Do not focus your attention, therefore, on him who was then born in Bethlehem, but worship him who from eternity has been begotten by the Father. Do not tolerate anyone who says that the Son began to exist at some point in time, but you must recognize that the Father is a timeless principle, a principle that has nothing to do with a temporal, unfathomable Son, himself without beginning: in short, the Father30, source of the river of justice, of the Only Begotten, whom he begot as he only knows. Do you want to know that our Lord Jesus Christ is also eternal king? Listen to him again when he says: “Your father Abraham rejoiced at the thought of seeing my Day; He saw it and was glad" (Jn 8:56). But as the Jews hardened in the face of this, he told them something even harsher: "Before Abraham existed, I Am" (8:58). And, in turn, he says to the Father: "Now, Father, glorify me, together with you, with the glory that was at your side before the world was" (Jn 17:5). He clearly said it: Before the world was, I had glory with you. And he says in turn: "... you loved me before the creation of the world" (17, 24).

21. Let us believe, therefore, "in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, who was born of the Father as true God before all ages, and by whom "all things were made" (Jn 1:3)": "Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers, all things were created by him" (Col 1:16), and none of the created things is removed from his power. Silence all heresy that speaks of various agents and authors of the world; restrain the tongue that smites Christ the Son of God with blasphemies; Let those who say that the sun is the Christ remain silent, because he is not this bright sun, but the creator of the sun; Let those who say that the world is the work of angels be silent, for they intend to invade what is the prerogative of the only Son. Both visible and invisible things, thrones and dominions (cf. Col 1:16), and "everything that has a name", all have been made by Christ. The Son reigns over the things that have been made by him, and not by taking the spoils of others but by exercising his lordship over his own works, as the evangelist John said: "Everything was made through her and without her nothing was made that exists" (Jn 1:3). Everything has been done by him, the Father acting through the Son.

22. I would like to give an example of what is said, although I know it is a weak example. For which of the visible things can be a suitable example of the invisible divine power? It is claimed, however, as a weak example, set by a weak person to the weak. It is, for example, as if a king who has a son who is also king along with him, and wishing to found a city, places before him a model of the city he is to build. The son, with the model, will bring the project to completion. In the same way, when the Father wanted to do all things, the Son was the one who did everything in obedience to the Father, so that this obedience preserves unscathed for the Father the freedom of his supreme power, but the Son has dominion over the things that he has made: in this way the Father's dominion over the things that he has made is not lowered nor does the Son obtain power over things made by another, but over those that he himself has founded. For it was not the angels who founded the world - this has already been spoken31 - but the only begotten Son begotten, as we said, before all ages. Through him everything was made, without excluding anything from his creative activity. And everything up to this point may be said for us by the grace of Christ.

23. Returning now to the confession of faith, let us conclude these words. Everything was done by Christ, the angels, the archangels, the dominions and the thrones. It is not that the Father lacked sufficient power to create by himself, but that he wanted the Son to reign over the things he had made, showing him the order of the things that were to be created. For the Only Begotten says, paying honor to his Father: «The Son can do nothing on his own, except what he sees the Father doing; What he does, the Son also does” (Jn 5:19). And in turn: "My Father works until now, and I also work" (Jn 5:17). There is no contradiction between the actions of both. “All that is mine is yours and all that is yours is mine” (Jn 17:10), says the Lord in the Gospel. This can be known clearly, both from the Old and New Testaments. For he who says: "Let us make man in our image and likeness" (Gen 1:26) was addressing someone who was clearly present. But the one who speaks most clearly (in this sense) is the psalmist, who says: "He said it, and it was; He commanded it, and they were created»32, as if the Father commanded and said, and the Son executed everything according to his desires. Job also said this, in a mystical sense: «He only spread out the Heavens and trodden the back of the Sea (Job 9,8), meaning with this to the intelligent that the one who, being here, walked on the sea was the one who had previously made the heavens33. And, for his part, the Lord says: "Was it you34 who took the earth as clay and made a living being, who, endowed with the power of speech, placed on the earth?" (Job 38,14 LXX). And, a little further down: «Have you been shown the doors of Death? Have you seen the gates to the land of Shadow? (38,17). With this he declares that the one who, through his goodness, descended into hell is the one who from the beginning made man from clay.

24. Christ is, therefore, the only begotten Son of God and author of the world. For "he was in the world, and the world was made through him" (Jn 1:10). And “he came to his house” (1:11), as the Gospel teaches us. Christ is not the author, in union with the Father, only of the things that are seen, but also of those that are not seen. For "in him, according to the Apostle, all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers: everything was created by him and for him, he exists prior to everything, and everything has its consistency in him" (Col 1:16-17). Even if you refer to the centuries35, the author of these, in obedience to the Father, is also Jesus Christ, since "in these last times he has spoken to us through the Son whom he appointed heir of all, through whom he also made the worlds" (Hebrews 1:2). To whom be glory, honor and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and forever and ever. Amen...

1. Until Hebrews 1:4 the text reads: «... whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the worlds; who being the brightness of his glory and the imprint of his substance, and the one who sustains everything with his powerful word, after carrying out the purification of sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, with a superiority over the angels that is all the greater as he surpasses them in the name that he has inherited. Of all this. which forms like the prologue of the letter to the Hebrews, the present catechesis seems to take shape to make an exposition on the eternal generation, from the Father, of the Logos, the Word of God that has been addressed to us in a more definitive way than the Prophets. The identity of nature between the Son and the Father also gives this catechesis a very clear anti-Arian imprint based on great fidelity to the meaning of the Symbol of faith.

3. The gospel of Matthew, which distributes its various sections in an almost didactic way, agrees with Mc and Lk in that this episode of the "profession of faith" is like a milestone in the middle of the gospel narrative. Jesus' contacts with the masses who have been following him in the first period of his public activity have diminished, but Mt 16:13-17 (leaving aside the question of primacy in 18-20) is the first unequivocal expression, on the part of the apostles, of the reality of Jesus as Son. Perhaps it is interesting to note that from now on Jesus will dedicate himself more intensely to the formation of the group of apostles. This is seen quite clearly in numerous passages in the chapters. 18-20 of Matthew. On the other hand, the recognition of Jesus as the Son of God is linked to the "first announcement" of the Passion (Mt 16,21: "From then on...") and to the explanation that whoever is a disciple of Jesus follows a path similar to his (16,24-26), although in the transfiguration (17,1-8) a prefiguration of the resurrection is offered.

"), rather a part of Ps 82:6 is used to highlight the Jews' rejection of Christ. 10. The catechesis develops from here to the end, with extraordinary prolixity, everything that can be said about the eternal generation of the Son by the Father. Also mentioned, for example, is the intervention of the Son in the creation of angels, Thrones, Dominions, etc., and, in general agreement with Col 1:15-20, his action in the creation of the universe, (cf. especially number 12 and note 17). These ideas, widely presented, extend to the end of the catechesis, which is why the epigraphs are deleted. The fact that the exposition is repetitive is probably the reason why only the first five paragraphs are included in Br. Albino Ortega's edition. However, the complete reproduction is of interest, since it is an excellent testimony of ecclesiastical orthodoxy following the footsteps of the Council of Nicaea. It thus allows us to see the identity of nature between the Son and the Father.
11. Of Jn 1:13, the possible plural reading of the original text is preferred ("They... were born... were born..."), simply because it is more in line with the flow of ideas.

12. The Greek "hypostasis" is translated as subsistence (which would be equivalent to the philosophical Latin term "suppositum"). It is something like "what underlies in the background" and indicates an idea of ​​its own consistency, which is what has allowed the distinction of three hypostases or subsistences in God and which in the Western Latin tradition have been called persons. Thus we speak of three different persons in God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

13. Eph 4:10 must be seen in the context of at least 4:7-10 (or 7-13), as the action of Christ distributing his gifts by descending into human misery and returning to the glory of the Father. A careful examination of the entire text allows us to relate the incarnation and redemption of men with their free enrichment through gifts and charismas.

30. In the theological tradition and in the ecclesiastical Magisterium, the Father has been called "beginning without beginning", while the Son has been described as "beginning of beginning". See, for example, the Bull Cantate Domino, of the Council of Florence, year 1442, para. 2 (DenzingerSchönmetzer, no. 1,331).
31. Reference has been made to this in no. 21.

32. The "let us do" in Gen 1:26 is interpreted as the plural agent Father and Son, and in the quote made here "he commanded" is understood as the Father "commanding" the Son to create. In any case, both texts are understood as a direct intervention of the Son in creation, which is what Cyril is interested in highlighting here.
33. Cyril possibly means: the same Jesus who, in the gospels, walks on the water of the sea (Mt 14:25 par) is the one who had also intervened in the creation of the heavens.
